name: Blacksmithing
prompt: Blacksmithing is a craft proficiency earned by years at the forge: the character can read the color of metal by heat (straw, purple, cherry, orange — each a different working temperature), shape hot iron with hammer and anvil, forge and repair weapons, tools and fittings, and tell by weight and sound whether a blade is sound or cracked. A proficient blacksmith can reforge a ruined sword into a working one with a fire, a hammer and patience, sharpen and balance any edge, and make a reasonable judgment about any metalwork they are shown — the quality of a lock, the age of a chain, whether a gate's hinges will hold. The craft's limits are honest: without the right metal and enough time, they can maintain and mend but not create exotica, and a masterwork blade still needs masterwork steel. When narrating, ground the proficiency in the physical work: the ring of a well-struck edge, the hiss of quenching steel in oil, the character's calloused hands doing small, precise things without looking — competence shown in the hands, not declared.
observation: I watched a blacksmith at work and got an ironclad idea — I wanted this one to be shown in the hands, not declared

name: Swordsmanship
prompt: Swordsmanship is a combat proficiency earned through long, repetitive training with a blade: the character has a trained grip, a trained guard and a trained habit of distance. They fight from a stable stance, keep their weapon where they know it is, and read an opponent's shoulders and hips before the swing arrives — they see the attack starting, not the attack landing. A proficient swordfighter does not win by being stronger or faster than the enemy; they win by being earlier and by not making the mistakes the enemy is waiting for: no wide recoveries, no empty flanks, no blade that ends up in the wrong place after a miss. They can fight in formation, duel one on one, and hold a line, and they know the honest limits of the skill — a trained sword does not beat five untrained attackers, and skill cannot fix a broken wrist. They also recognize other styles: they will notice a brawler, a duelist and a soldier by how they hold the blade, and they adjust their distance accordingly. When narrating, keep the skill in the mechanics: the quiet shift of weight before a cut, the parry that answers without being seen, the way the character fights economically, spending nothing they do not have to spend — and when the skill is enough, let it read as calm rather than heroic.
observation: I wanted a fighting skill that reads as calm and economical — the trained person who is earlier, not the superhero who is faster

name: Lockpicking
prompt: Lockpicking is a fine-motor proficiency earned by patient practice with picks and tension wrenches: the character can feel, through the pick, the individual pins of a lock and can work them free in the right order. A proficient picker can open a standard lock quietly, with no damage, in a matter of minutes, can tell by the feel of the mechanism what kind of lock they are dealing with and roughly how well made it is, and can usually open a lock without leaving a trace that it was touched. The limits of the skill are the lock's quality: a well-made lock slows a good picker down and a masterwork lock may defeat them entirely, and some locks — warded, keyed-different, or magical — are simply not something a pick can answer. Picking is also a knowledge of what should not be opened: a character with this skill can tell the difference between a door that is locked for security and a door that is locked because what is behind it must not be disturbed, and they know which kind they are standing in front of. When narrating, keep it small and tense: the click of a pin dropping, the breath held, the faint scratch of steel, and the moment the key turns on its own — competence in a quiet, close-in scene, not an action beat.
observation: I wanted the quiet, close-in version of competence — the locked door as a scene, not a stat roll

name: Herbalism
prompt: Herbalism is a field proficiency earned through study and long practice in the field: the character can identify hundreds of plants by leaf, bark, root, flower and smell, and knows which ones heal, which ones poison, which ones are food, which ones are dyes and which ones are simply dangerous to touch. A proficient herbalist can find useful plants in the wild and prepare them correctly — a poultice that draws infection, a tincture that holds a fever down, a draught that numbs pain — and can recognize when a preparation is wrong, spoiled, or counterfeit, by smell, color and the way it behaves. The skill is knowledge of limits, not a cure-all: an herbalist can treat wounds, fever and simple ailments with the right plants and the right time, but they cannot set a broken bone, stop a deep infection, or do anything a real physician's hands cannot, and a plant used wrong is just a poison with a prettier name. The character also knows what not to touch, which is often the most important thing they know in the field. When narrating, ground the skill in the field: the character rubbing a leaf between their fingers, the way they crouch and look before they pick, the quiet confidence of someone who has learned the plants by season — competence shown in the hands and the eyes, not declared.
observation: I wanted a field skill that is knowledge of limits — the plant that heals is the same plant that kills, and the character knows the line

name: Horseback Riding
prompt: Horseback Riding is an equestrian proficiency earned by long, daily practice with horses: the character can mount, dismount, turn, stop and steady a horse with their body and their hands, and can keep their balance and their composure when the animal is spooked, tired, or frightened. A proficient rider can ride at a long gallop over rough ground without being thrown, handle a horse in narrow or crowded spaces, and read a horse's mood by its ears, its breath and the way it carries its weight — they know a horse that is about to bolt, a horse that is in pain, and a horse that has simply had enough. The skill covers the honest limits of the animal: a rider cannot make a tired horse run, cannot make a frightened horse brave, and cannot ride a horse that is injured without it showing in how the ride goes. A good rider also knows the basics of horse care — feeding, water, the sound a healthy horse makes and the one it does not — and knows when to rest an animal, which is the difference between a horse that gets them there and a horse that dies on the way. When narrating, keep the skill in the partnership: the small shifts of the rider's weight, the quiet word to a spooked animal, the way a good horse and a good rider move as one thing — and when the horse is tired or frightened, let that show honestly, because the skill includes knowing when the animal has reached its limit.
observation: I wanted a skill that is a partnership, not a vehicle — the rider's job is to know when the horse has had enough

name: Sailing
prompt: Sailing is a seafaring proficiency earned by long service on water: the character reads the wind, the water and the sky well enough to take a boat from one safe place to another and back, in fair weather and in weather that is not. A proficient sailor can handle a working boat — rig the lines, set the canvas, steer by the sound the hull makes against the water — and can judge distance, depth and current by the look of the water and the behavior of the birds. They know the honest limits of the craft: a good sailor cannot beat a headwind, cannot take a small boat into open water in a storm, and cannot read a coast that has never been read before without the sound of the depth sounding and the look of the water telling them what is there. They also know what the sea is like when it is not kind, and they do not gamble with it. The skill is knowledge of when to go, when to wait, and when to turn back, and a competent sailor is recognized by how often they turn back. When narrating, ground the skill in the water and the wind: the creak of the lines, the sound of the keel against the current, the way the character reads the sky before anyone else has thought to look — competence shown in the hands on the rope and the eyes on the water, not declared.
observation: I wanted a skill that is knowing when to turn back — the competent sailor is recognized by how often they refuse to sail

name: Cartography
prompt: Cartography is a study proficiency earned through careful practice with compass, chain and pencil: the character can read a map the way a sailor reads the water — not as a picture of a place but as a record of what someone measured, when, and how well — and they can make a map of a place they have walked, at a scale that is useful, with the soundings, the tracks, the water sources and the dangerous ground marked where they actually are. A proficient cartographer can hold a bearing, estimate distance by pace and by landmark, and find their way across open or unfamiliar ground by the relationship between what they see and what the map says should be there. They know the honest limits of the craft: a map is only as good as the last person who checked it, a bearing drifts if the compass is not trusted, and a coastline changes after a storm. They also know what a map is for — not to decorate a wall but to make a decision: where to cross, where to camp, where not to go — and they will tell a party that is reading a map the wrong way, and they will say it plainly. When narrating, keep the skill in the small, precise work: the pencil checking a line, the compass held level, the character's finger tracing a route that is already half decided — competence shown in the attention, not declared.
observation: I wanted a study skill that is a tool for decisions — the map is not the place, it is the record of what someone measured, and the character knows when to trust it
